transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Sarah Patel (CTO - Stellar Retail), Ben Carter (Lead ML Eng), Nina Gomez (Product), Aaron Lee (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics: streaming, important params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), and retry/backoff behavior. Customer concerned about latency (95th ms), cost, and PII handling. Discussed Redwood Console and Optimize features (batching/caching suggestions) and next steps for POC scoping.

Topics:
- Hosted API quickstart and model selection
- Streaming responses and partial outputs
- Important generation params and best-practices
- Retry strategies, idempotency, and backoff for intermittent failures
- Console overview: logs, token cost breakdown, routes
- Optimize suggestions: batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization recommendations
- Security: data retention, SOC2, encryption, KMS/VPC notes

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off in a minute but just to intro myself and Luis in case folks haven't met us, I'm Maya Chen, account exec for the retail vertical at Redwood.
[00:08] Sarah: Hi Maya, Sarah here, thanks for putting this together.
[00:10] Ben: Ben Carter, hey, excited to see the streaming bit.
[00:13] Maya: Great, Luis is our solutions engineer, he'll walk through the demo and I'll jump in for pricing/next steps.
[00:18] Luis: Hey all, quick plan: 1) hosted API basics, 2) live demo showing chat stream + params, 3) retry behavior and patterns, 4) short Console glance, then q&a. Sound good?
[00:26] Nina: Sounds great.
[00:28] Aaron: Yep.
[00:30] Luis: Cool, starting with the API: it's standard REST/SDK call, you pass model, messages or prompt, and set params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and streaming flag. We'll demo both a non-stream and stream. Also talk about best-practice defaults for retail use cases.
[00:45] Ben: Quick question, we care a lot about 95th percentile latency for customer-facing chat. Do you have numbers for hosted models?
[00:52] Maya: We publish verified performance profiles in the model catalog; for mid-sized models you can expect median ~80-150ms per token in our hosted tier and 95th around 300-400ms depending on sequence length. We'll send a spreadsheet with tuned profiles.
[01:05] Sarah: Okay, that's helpful — our SLO is 500ms 95th for short queries.
[01:10] Luis: Good, that'll fit. Demo time: I'll share my screen.
[01:16] [SCREEN SHARED]
[01:20] Luis: Here's a simple curl example: POST /v1/chat/completions with streaming=true. We open a chunked HTTP stream and you get partial delta tokens in near real-time. This is great for UX where you want immediate typing indicators.
[01:35] [00:35] Luis: I'll run a sample prompt: 'help me write a quick product description for this shoe — 40 words max' with streaming on.
[01:40] [00:40] Transcript glitch: 'shoo' instead of 'shoe' in auto caption, ignore that.
[01:44] [00:44] Luis: Streaming output arrives as server-sent events chunks, you can render token-by-token. We also emit interim metadata events for finish_reason and token counts.
[01:54] Ben: If a streaming connection drops mid-response, how do we handle it? Resume? Retry?
[01:58] Luis: Good question. Current pattern is: for idempotent requests (stateless prompts) you can retry with the same prompt — you may get a slightly different completion due to sampling. For deterministic needs, we recommend using temperature=0 and/or sending a seed; also our SDK supports resumed streams for some SDKs and we provide a request-id in headers to correlate. If you need strict resume-from-token semantics that's part of our roadmap.
[02:25] Sarah: Hm okay we do care about determinism in some flows.
[02:29] Luis: For most customer-facing chat, UX mitigates small diffs. For generation important for compliance or billing, we advise server-side logging of full completions and deterministic settings.
[02:38] Nina: Can you walk params — temperature and top_p quick? We have content teams who tune these frequently.
[02:42] Luis: Sure. Temperature controls randomness; 0 is greedy, 1 is default-ish, lower = safer. top_p is nucleus sampling — you can use either. We usually recommend starting at temperature 0.2-0.6 for product copy, and use max_tokens to bound cost. Also set stop sequences to avoid trailing text.
[02:56] [03:00] Luis: Here's an example JSON payload we use in the SDK for chat: model, messages, temperature:0.3, max_tokens:60, stream:true. You can stream and still receive the final 'finish' meta.
[03:10] Ben: About retries — if the API returns a 503 because of a transient capacity issue what's recommended? Exponential backoff?
[03:15] Luis: Yes, exponential backoff with jitter. Our client SDKs implement retries for 5xx and 429 with progressive backoff. For streaming, if the stream fails mid-response, we recommend reconciling with the last fully received completion; then re-request. Also we expose a per-request idempotency key header for safe retry semantics for stateful operations.
[03:36] Aaron: Does the SDK expose token-level billing so we can estimate cost per request?
[03:39] Maya: Console shows token-level cost and breakdown per route. We also have per-request metadata you can log for analytic joins.
[03:46] Luis: Quick note on batching/caching: Redwood Optimize suggests batching small requests when latency budget allows, and prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts (like product metadata) which can reduce per-token spend significantly.
[03:58] Ben: For our use case we have many short assistant prompts and a few long form copy tasks. Batching sounds risky for interactive chat.
[04:04] Luis: Right — for interactive chat you typically avoid batching at the UI level, but server-side you can batch background jobs or reranking. Caching is usually the best win for repeated fixed prompts — e.g., canonical product blurb.
[04:15] [04:20] Nina: Can you show the Console?
[04:22] [SCREEN: REDWOOD CONSOLE]
[04:24] Luis: Console: per-route dashboards, latency percentiles, token usage, and streaming request logs. You can filter by model version, region, and customer route. Here we also show suggestions from Optimize for quantization or lower-cost model variants based on workload.
[04:40] Sarah: On security — we have to be SOC2 and ISO aligned and want audit logs and KMS. How does hosted handle keys and retention?
[04:48] Maya: Our hosted offering is SOC2 compliant; we have audit logs, RBAC, and integrations with customer KMS for Private deployments. Hosted keeps transcripts for X days by default but offers configurable retention and redaction policies; we'll share our security whitepaper.
[05:02] Ben: Data residency? Some of our EU customers must keep data in EU.
[05:06] Maya: We support region pinning for requests and can route to EU regions. For strict residency you may want Redwood Private (VPC) — we'll outline tradeoffs in the POC scoping.
[05:15] Aaron: Any PII scrubbing recommendation?
[05:17] Luis: We recommend client-side scrubbing and server-side redaction hooks; Console shows options and webhooks for ingestion-time processing.
[05:25] [05:30] Luis: Back to the streaming specifics — implementation note: streaming reduces perceived latency, but you pay for tokens generated. If you stream partial tokens you might incur more smaller charges but overall cost is tied to tokens returned. Also watch for early stop sequences to avoid extra tokens.
[05:42] Ben: For model selection — we want decent quality but cost matters. Do you recommend a family/size?
[05:47] Luis: For retail chat we often recommend mid-tier open models (balance of speed/cost) or Redwood-curated variants. Console includes curated profiles; Optimize can recommend quantized variants if accuracy tolerant.
[05:59] Nina: Do you support function/tool calling for structured outputs?
[06:02] Luis: Yes — our hosted API supports function calls and structured output spec. You can define schema and the model will emit JSON-like responses; Console will parse and surface these in logs.
[06:14] [06:20] Sarah: What about rate limits and burst policy?
[06:23] Maya: Hosted has rate limits per account, and we can offer burst increases in Dedicated or contractual tiers. We'll share quota docs.
[06:30] Ben: Any notes on glue with our infra — e.g., VPC peering for Private?
[06:34] Maya: For Private we do VPC peering or on-prem connectors, plus KMS integrations. For hosted we use secure TLS in transit and standard encryption at rest.
[06:44] Luis: I'll demo a short SDK snippet showing streaming with retry handling.
[06:48] [SCREEN: CODE SNIPPET]
[06:50] Luis: Pseudocode: open stream, on chunk append to buffer, if error do exponential backoff and retry using request-id; on complete emit final. SDKs abstract much of this.
[07:02] Ben: If we re-request after a mid-stream drop, do we get duplicate tokens?
[07:06] Luis: Potentially yes — that's why we include idempotency keys and recommend client reconciliation (dedupe by final text or use sequence tokens if available).
[07:14] Nina: On monitoring we need to tie model regressions back to prompts — do you support evals or set-based regressions?
[07:19] Luis: Redwood Optimize has prompt-set monitoring and quality regression alerts; you provide eval sets and the system alerts on drift or quality drops. We can tie that to rollouts so you don't push broken models.
[07:30] Sarah: Cost control: how do you recommend keeping cost predictable for production?
[07:34] Maya: Use per-route budgets, token caps, and quota alerts in Console. Also Implement caching and use lower-cost model variants for non-critical tasks. Optimize can recommend model profiles by route.
[07:46] Aaron: Can the SDK do client-side token counting to predict cost?
[07:49] Luis: We provide tokenizers and client-side token estimation to help cap requests before they hit the API.
[07:55] [08:00] Maya: We're about halfway — do you want to dig deeper into any area?
[08:03] Ben: Could we get a short POC to test streaming under our load? We'd like to run simulated concurrent chat traffic and measure 95th.
[08:10] Maya: Absolutely, typical POC is 2-4 weeks, Redwood SE helps with scripts and we run benchmarks together. We'll scope dedicated capacity if needed.
[08:18] Luis: We'll need sample payloads, expected concurrency, and SLOs.
[08:21] Ben: I'll send concurrency matrix and sample prompts.
[08:24] Maya: Great. A few clarifying Qs from Nina?
[08:26] Nina: For our content team we want reproducible longform generation. Should we do temperature 0 and store completions?
[08:31] Luis: Yes, temperature=0 plus logging completions server-side. Also pin model version in requests so you don't get roll-forward drift.
[08:38] Sarah: Any contractual SLA for hosted?
[08:40] Maya: Hosted has best-effort; Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime SLAs. We can discuss Dedicated if you want contractual guarantees.
[08:50] Ben: What's the onboarding timeline? We have internal stakeholders who want this in prod within quarter.
[08:55] Maya: Typical timeline: quickstart and bench in 1-2 weeks, POC 2-4 weeks, then staging/rollout. If you need faster, Dedicated commitments shorten runway.
[09:07] [09:10] Luis: Quick follow-up demo: show SDK streaming retry snippet with sample backoff code.
[09:15] [SCREEN: CODE + RUN]
[09:18] Luis: Running a small simulated burst, you can see how the SDK retries transient 503s and logs each attempt in Console.
[09:28] Ben: Nice, do you provide sample load scripts?
[09:30] Luis: Yes, SE repo has scripts we can share for load/latency tests.
[09:34] Sarah: Ok. Couple of security items we'll ask for: SOC2 report, data retention policy, and encryption details.
[09:40] Maya: We'll attach security pack in follow-up email.
[09:43] Nina: On function calling again, how do you guarantee output shape? Our downstream processors expect strict JSON schemas.
[09:49] Luis: Use function schema binding in the API and validate in Console logs; for strict needs add an extra validation layer or use temperature 0 to improve consistency.
[09:58] [10:00] Maya: We should recap and list next steps.
[10:03] Maya: Recap: we'll share pricing/latency spreadsheet, security docs, and SE will prepare demo workspace and load scripts. Ben to share payloads and SLOs. Then schedule POC scoping call.
[10:15] Ben: Yep I'll send payloads by EOD Thursday (3/05).
[10:18] Maya: Great, I'll send pricing and schedule the scoping for week of 3/9.
[10:22] Sarah: Thanks all, that was useful.
[10:24] Luis: Thanks, everyone.
[10:26] [END]
